name: Anti-Federalists
summary: The Anti-Federalists opposed ratifying the 1787 US Constitution as drafted, fearing it would consolidate the states into one distant national government. They held that free republics must be small, that representatives should be numerous, close to and dependent on ordinary citizens, and that rulers, standing armies and federal taxing power threaten liberty unless limited by explicit rights. Their pressure helped produce the Bill of Rights.
scope: The 1787-88 opponents of ratifying the US Constitution, as the defining sources present them: Storing and Dry's collection of the Anti-Federalist writings (the Brutus and Federal Farmer essays, Centinel, Agrippa, the Pennsylvania minority's Dissent, the speeches of Patrick Henry and Melancton Smith), the Encyclopedia of Federalism, and the Bill of Rights Institute essay after Storing. These sources describe 'a philosophy about government' and a preferred structure of society: a confederation of largely self-governing states, small republics with numerous representatives close to the people, and written guarantees of rights, with leaders such as Patrick Henry, George Mason, Richard Henry Lee and Melancton Smith. It covers the ratification-era debate (1787-89) and the Anti-Federalist Party the Encyclopedia of Federalism dates to 1789-1800 is left out as a later party; economic, social and modern questions were mostly not addressed in these texts.
